
::: {.src}
@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen; @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms
:::

::: notes
Here is the vocabulary of the session as one grid, in the words of the glossary that Nosek and colleagues wrote for the SCORE programme. The question stays the same throughout, and what varies is the data and the analysis. The same data and the same analysis is reproducibility: if I rerun your recipe, do I get your number? The same data under a different, justifiable analysis is robustness, which asks whether your finding survives my defensible choices. The same analysis on new data is replicability. The fourth cell, new data and a new analysis at once, is generalisability, and we leave it aside. Everything that follows refers back to this grid. You reproduce a result before the break, you spend the second half on robustness, and we end on a replication of this very paper.
:::

## Multi100 from the inside {#multi100-from-the-inside .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Multi100 gave one claim from each of 100 published studies to at least five independent analysts, and I was one of the five on this claim
- What arrived: the **published paper** in full, its **central claim** in one sentence, and a pointer to the **data**, sixteen Eurobarometer waves that each analyst fetched from GESIS under licence. No instruction on method
- **Task 1**, a free reanalysis ending in one categorical conclusion; months later **Task 2**, one main result under four instructions: a single test statistic, the contextual variables of the paper set aside, the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** as the outcome and the **unemployment rate** as the predictor
- Every statistic was converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a **Cohen's *d***, so that five models in two software languages could be read on one axis
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two things stayed hidden throughout: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; the Multi100 preregistration, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–8.
:::

::: notes
Multi100 took one claim from each of a hundred published studies and gave it to at least five independent analysts, and I was one of the five on this claim. What arrived was the paper, the claim in one sentence lifted from the abstract, and a pointer to the data, sixteen Eurobarometer waves that each analyst fetched from GESIS under licence. No instruction on method: any analysis that you could defend. The work came in two tasks: a free reanalysis ending in one categorical verdict, and months later one main result under four instructions, which fixed the outcome and the predictor, set aside the contextual variables of the paper, and left everything else to us. Every statistic was then converted to a partial correlation and a Cohen's d, so that five models could be read on one axis. [advance] And two things stayed hidden: who the others were, and what they were finding.
:::

## The five results {#the-five-results .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: forest5
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# Copied from _segments/eu-frames/_p1-multi100.qmd (chunk forest5).
# The five Multi100 analysts of the same claim (cases/eu-frames/data/reference_marks.csv, with
# the software and document format from cases/eu-frames/data/analysts5.csv), each placed on
# the degrees of freedom of its own inference; an open circle marks the value
# in the Multi100 record where it differs, which is PRL47 alone, converted on
# its respondent count. C6HJR highlighted. The label shows the software and
# the document format of each analysis.
tools5 <- analysts5 |> dplyr::select(id = analyst_id, tool, document)
fa <- ref_marks |>
  dplyr::filter(id != "OA") |>
  dplyr::left_join(tools5, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    me      = id == "C6HJR",
    lab     = paste0(id, "   ", tool, "  ", document),
    differs = abs(r_recorded - r_placement) > 0.001
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(r_placement) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = lab))
fa_rec <- dplyr::filter(fa, differs)

ggplot2::ggplot(fa, ggplot2::aes(r_placement, lab)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded, xend = r_placement, yend = lab),
               colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded), shape = 21, size = 5.5,
             colour = grey_mid, fill = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded, label = sprintf("recorded %s", fmt_num(r_recorded))),
            vjust = -1.3, hjust = 1.05, size = 4, colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = me), size = 6) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = paste("r =", fmt_num(r_placement, 2))),
            hjust = 1.3, size = 4.5, colour = ncl_blue) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = ncl_blue, `TRUE` = orange)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.62, 0.06), labels = \(x) fmt_num(x, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "partial correlation r, on the degrees of freedom of each inference",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15)
```

::: {.small}
- All five estimates negative, with partial *r* from **`r fmt_num(min(five_r), 2)` to `r fmt_num(max(five_r), 2)`** on the degrees of freedom of each inference, and one of the five not significant even by the errors of its own model
- Multi100 recorded PRL47 at *r* = `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "r_recorded"))` (open circle), because its *z* was converted on `r fmt_n(analysts5$n[analysts5$analyst_id == "PRL47"])` respondents
:::

::: {.src}
Task 2 results as recorded in the public Multi100 dataset (osf.io/q5h2c); PRL47 placed on the `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "df_placement"), 1)` Satterthwaite df of a course refit of its design (cases/eu-frames/data/reference_marks.csv).
:::

::: notes
Here are the five of us, on this one claim. All five found a negative association, so on direction we were unanimous. On size: from minus point zero six at the top, which is not significant even by the errors of its own model, to minus point four five, more than seven times as large. The orange dot is me, at minus point two four. Now the open circle on the row of PRL47, the value that Multi100 recorded, minus point zero zero six, because its z statistic was converted on the number of respondents, as if every respondent were an independent test of a national unemployment rate. The filled dot puts the same statistic on the degrees of freedom of a refit of its design, close to my own result. As recorded, the spread looked like two orders of magnitude, mostly from the conversion; the rest is what the second half is about.
:::
